bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Construction and project execution delays — Flagged as a Business Risk in the MD&A risk-mitigation table: delays in new hotel construction or expansion of existing properties can increase construction costs, extend timelines and reduce revenue streams, ultimately impacting the ability to achieve growth and profitability. This is structurally significant given 43 hotels and 3,958 keys under development and active projects at EM Bypass Kolkata, Juhu Mumbai, Visakhapatnam, Pune and Navi Mumbai.
- Seasonality of hospitality demand — Flagged as a Business Risk in the MD&A risk table: the hospitality industry is inherently seasonal, with revenue, profit margins and earnings fluctuating with demand across the year. The business is heavily reliant on peak travel seasons, producing variations in cash flow and profitability and requiring reliance on alternative revenue streams during slower periods.
- Single-activity and single-sector concentration — 100% of turnover comes from Accommodation and Food Service (BRSR Section A), split 49.54% Accommodation, 43.66% Food and Beverage and 6.80% Other Services, leaving no diversification outside hospitality to buffer a sector downturn.
- Geographic concentration in India with no international footprint — All 42 hotels are national, across 15 states and 3 Union Territories, with no international locations and exports not applicable. Flurys is further concentrated, with 84 of 110 outlets in West Bengal. Performance is therefore fully exposed to Indian demand, policy and weather conditions.
- High employee attrition and talent dependence — Permanent-employee turnover was 49% in FY 2025-26 (100% in each of FY 2024-25 and FY 2023-24), against a workforce of 4,172 employees of whom 1,921 are other-than-permanent. Service delivery in a design-led luxury and boutique hospitality model depends on retaining trained staff.
- F&B supply-chain and input-cost exposure — The MD&A Logistics section states the business relies on daily or weekly inflows of high-quality perishable raw material and must navigate inventory shortages, price volatility linked to weather patterns, seasonality, exchange-rate fluctuations and import tariffs, while dependence on third-party delivery platforms for off-premise dining adds an external technology and last-mile dependency.
- Operating-cost inflation, energy and utility exposure — The Chairperson's statement cites inflationary trends in operating costs and intermittent supply-side constraints including LPG shortage in select markets; the MD&A notes higher per-unit electricity cost and higher fuel prices, and the outlook warns that geopolitical developments may keep fuel, logistics and utility costs elevated.
- Geopolitical and travel-disruption risk — Management cites restive geopolitics, disruption in domestic travel in April and May and frequent fluctuations in travel sentiment; the MD&A outlook warns that West Asia tensions and related aviation disruptions may temporarily affect select international and corporate travel corridors, with West Asia conflict duration a key determinant of global growth, inflation and financial stability.
- Industry supply additions and competitive intensity — Key industry drivers include incremental room supply alongside demand; ICRA projects supply growth of 5-6% against demand growth of 8-10% CAGR, and sector growth is normalising to approximately 6-8% with ICRA revising its outlook from Positive to Stable. In foodservice, independent outlets hold 64.8% share and the MD&A cites intense competition from unorganised players as a key industry challenge.
- Margin dilution from the retail F&B mix shift — Management states that the EBITDA margin moderation from 33.0% in FY 2024-25 to 30.8% reflects a deliberate decision to fast-track Flurys, which operates at a comparatively lower margin — a structural mix risk as F&B grows towards 43% of revenue and the Flurys store count is targeted to more than triple by the end of the decade.
- Cyber-security and data-privacy exposure — The Company maintains a Cyber Security Policy with privacy provisions, and one cyber-security consumer complaint was received during FY 2025-26 (nil in FY 2024-25). Exposure rises with the SAP S/4HANA rollout, cloud-based ERP, contactless check-in, QR-based payments and a loyalty database of 2,40,000 members.
- Environmental compliance at ecologically sensitive sites — The Park Visakhapatnam and one Goa unit operate in or around ecologically sensitive areas requiring environmental approvals/clearances; continued compliance is a condition of operation, and Visakhapatnam is simultaneously the site of a 100-room expansion.

outlook.body: ASPHL ended FY 2025-26 with 42 operational hotels and 2,677 keys across 32 cities, having added seven properties aggregating 283 keys during the year across leisure, pilgrimage and urban markets, including Zone by The Park properties in Darjeeling, Gangtok and Katra and Zone Connect by The Park Patna in Bihar. The flagship project of the year was the integrated hospitality-led development on EM Bypass, Kolkata, comprising a 218-key hotel and 69 serviced apartments under the new THE Park UNIZEN branded-residence model, which uses residential sales to support development of the hospitality asset; 29 of the 69 apartments (42% of residential inventory) were booked at an average realisation of INR 20,857 per sq. ft., and the project is expected to generate INR 300-350 crores of cash flows over the next three years. The under-development pipeline stands at 43 hotels and 3,958 keys — THE Park Hotels (9 hotels, 1,430 keys), THE Park Collection (3 hotels, 91 keys), Zone by The Park (17 hotels, 1,455 keys) and Zone Connect by The Park (14 hotels, 982 keys) — weighted towards asset-light formats with 31 managed (2,814 keys) versus 7 owned (997 keys) and 5 leased (147 keys), taking the total intended portfolio to 85 hotels and 6,635 keys by FY 2029-30. Strategic projects at EM Bypass Kolkata, Juhu Mumbai, Visakhapatnam and Navi Mumbai are all in active stages of development: the Juhu property targets a launch in H2 FY28, ground construction is underway in Visakhapatnam, and progress continues across Pune and Navi Mumbai. At THE Park Visakhapatnam, site preparation and landscaping works are underway for an expansion that will add 100 new hotel rooms, a signature lounge, a luxury spa and a modern fitness centre; at THE Park Chennai The Residence Floor is being completely refurbished, and the Goa hotels plan to widen their F&B offerings. Inorganic expansion during the year included acquiring a 90% stake in the Juhu property via Zillion Hotels and Resorts, acquiring Purity on Lake Vembanad (including a luxury houseboat asset) and signing The Malabar House in Fort Kochi, Kerala (transaction expected to complete by October 2026), plus the addition of a property in Tranquebar, Tamil Nadu — all extending THE Park Collection. In retail F&B, Flurys grew to 110 outlets (44 cafés, 14 restaurants, 52 kiosks across seven states) after adding 10 outlets during the year, is on track to reach 120 stores shortly with more than 30 outlets planned across Delhi NCR, Pune and Bengaluru, targets around 140 outlets within 10 months and 150 in FY 2026-27, and holds an ambition to reach 200 stores by 2028 and to more than triple its footprint by the end of the decade. Operational build-out included the enterprise-wide rollout of SAP S/4HANA and deployment of the Nor1 AI-enabled upselling platform, alongside expansion to 4 IGBC-certified hotels.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian hospitality sector expected to remain resilient in FY 2026-27 on sustained domestic leisure and MICE demand, with ICRA projecting 7-9% YoY revenue growth alongside continued improvement in occupancy and ARR
- ICRA projects hotel demand growth of 8-10% CAGR between FY 2024-25 and FY 2027-28, outpacing supply growth of 5-6%, with measured capacity additions expected to sustain healthy occupancy and ADR levels
- Sectoral growth normalising to approximately 6-8% in FY 2025-26 after three years of double-digit expansion, prompting ICRA to revise its outlook from Positive to Stable — a high-base effect rather than weakening underlying demand
- Structural drivers: rising discretionary spending, an expanding middle class, increasing business travel and India's growing prominence in the global economy supporting higher domestic and international travel demand
- Government initiatives — Swadesh Darshan 2.0, PRASHAD, RCS-UDAN, destination development and hospitality skilling — plus the GST reduction to 5% (without input tax credit) on hotel rooms priced up to INR 7,500 per day, expected to improve affordability and support mid-scale and budget demand
- Indian economic outlook for FY 2026-27 robust with real GDP growth projected at approximately 6.9% and CPI inflation around 4.6%; services expected to remain the primary growth engine, particularly financial services and hospitality
- Pilgrimage tourism scaling as a structured, high-yield economic driver, creating white space for quality stays near spiritual hubs such as Prayagraj, Darjeeling, Gangtok, Katra, Ayodhya and Ujjain
- MICE demand decentralising to cities such as Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kochi and Indore, increasing the requirement for event-ready hospitality in emerging conference cities
- The stay itself is now central to travel decisions — nearly 80% of Indian travellers prioritise accommodation and 84% plan to increase travel spending by 20-50%, favouring curated experiential stays; scaling premium inventory is engineered to maximise guest wallet-share, extend length of stay and optimise ARR
- India's destination wedding economy has grown to a USD 18 billion market with over 60% of premium weddings now destination-based, turning celebrations into high-margin room nights and ancillary revenue

risks.note: Flagged as a Business Risk in the MD&A risk-mitigation table: delays in new hotel construction or expansion of existing properties can increase construction costs, extend timelines and reduce revenue streams, ultimately impacting the ability to achieve growth and profitability. This is structurally significant given 43 hotels and 3,958 keys under development and active projects at EM Bypass Kolkata, Juhu Mumbai, Visakhapatnam, Pune and Navi Mumbai.

Flagged as a Business Risk in the MD&A risk table: the hospitality industry is inherently seasonal, with revenue, profit margins and earnings fluctuating with demand across the year. The business is heavily reliant on peak travel seasons, producing variations in cash flow and profitability and requiring reliance on alternative revenue streams during slower periods.

100% of turnover comes from Accommodation and Food Service (BRSR Section A), split 49.54% Accommodation, 43.66% Food and Beverage and 6.80% Other Services, leaving no diversification outside hospitality to buffer a sector downturn.

risks.risk: Geographic concentration in India with no international footprint
risks.note: All 42 hotels are national, across 15 states and 3 Union Territories, with no international locations and exports not applicable. Flurys is further concentrated, with 84 of 110 outlets in West Bengal. Performance is therefore fully exposed to Indian demand, policy and weather conditions.

risks.risk: High employee attrition and talent dependence
risks.note: Permanent-employee turnover was 49% in FY 2025-26 (100% in each of FY 2024-25 and FY 2023-24), against a workforce of 4,172 employees of whom 1,921 are other-than-permanent. Service delivery in a design-led luxury and boutique hospitality model depends on retaining trained staff.

The MD&A Logistics section states the business relies on daily or weekly inflows of high-quality perishable raw material and must navigate inventory shortages, price volatility linked to weather patterns, seasonality, exchange-rate fluctuations and import tariffs, while dependence on third-party delivery platforms for off-premise dining adds an external technology and last-mile dependency.

risks.risk: Operating-cost inflation, energy and utility exposure
risks.note: The Chairperson's statement cites inflationary trends in operating costs and intermittent supply-side constraints including LPG shortage in select markets; the MD&A notes higher per-unit electricity cost and higher fuel prices, and the outlook warns that geopolitical developments may keep fuel, logistics and utility costs elevated.

Management cites restive geopolitics, disruption in domestic travel in April and May and frequent fluctuations in travel sentiment; the MD&A outlook warns that West Asia tensions and related aviation disruptions may temporarily affect select international and corporate travel corridors, with West Asia conflict duration a key determinant of global growth, inflation and financial stability.

risks.risk: Industry supply additions and competitive intensity
risks.note: Key industry drivers include incremental room supply alongside demand; ICRA projects supply growth of 5-6% against demand growth of 8-10% CAGR, and sector growth is normalising to approximately 6-8% with ICRA revising its outlook from Positive to Stable. In foodservice, independent outlets hold 64.8% share and the MD&A cites intense competition from unorganised players as a key industry challenge.

risks.risk: Margin dilution from the retail F&B mix shift
risks.note: Management states that the EBITDA margin moderation from 33.0% in FY 2024-25 to 30.8% reflects a deliberate decision to fast-track Flurys, which operates at a comparatively lower margin — a structural mix risk as F&B grows towards 43% of revenue and the Flurys store count is targeted to more than triple by the end of the decade.

The Company maintains a Cyber Security Policy with privacy provisions, and one cyber-security consumer complaint was received during FY 2025-26 (nil in FY 2024-25). Exposure rises with the SAP S/4HANA rollout, cloud-based ERP, contactless check-in, QR-based payments and a loyalty database of 2,40,000 members.

risks.risk: Environmental compliance at ecologically sensitive sites
risks.note: The Park Visakhapatnam and one Goa unit operate in or around ecologically sensitive areas requiring environmental approvals/clearances; continued compliance is a condition of operation, and Visakhapatnam is simultaneously the site of a 100-room expansion.

- Structural drivers: rising discretionary spending, an expanding middle class, increasing business travel and India's growing prominence in the global economy supporting higher domestic and international travel demand
- Government initiatives — Swadesh Darshan 2.0, PRASHAD, RCS-UDAN, destination development and hospitality skilling — plus the GST reduction to 5% (without input tax credit) on hotel rooms priced up to INR 7,500 per day, expected to improve affordability and support mid-scale and budget demand
- Indian economic outlook for FY 2026-27 robust with real GDP growth projected at approximately 6.9% and CPI inflation around 4.6%; services expected to remain the primary growth engine, particularly financial services and hospitality
- Pilgrimage tourism scaling as a structured, high-yield economic driver, creating white space for quality stays near spiritual hubs such as Prayagraj, Darjeeling, Gangtok, Katra, Ayodhya and Ujjain
- MICE demand decentralising to cities such as Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kochi and Indore, increasing the requirement for event-ready hospitality in emerging conference cities

- Premiumisation of dining — India's premium casual and fine-dining segment growing at a 12-15% CAGR, supporting elevated F&B concepts across the portfolio and Flurys
- Indian foodservice industry projected to reach USD 153.37 billion by 2031 at a 10.3% CAGR, with cloud kitchens, delivery-led models and chained restaurants growing fastest
- AI is reshaping travel planning — around 83% of Indian travellers find AI eases planning, and India's AI-in-tourism market is set to grow from ~USD 109 million to ~USD 595 million by 2030 (32.6% CAGR), creating appetite for AI-discoverable hospitality
- Sustainability becoming a booking priority, with about 87% of Indian travellers wanting eco-conscious habits and clear eco-labels — favouring brands with credible eco-credentials

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: ASPHL ended FY 2025-26 with 42 operational hotels and 2,677 keys across 32 cities, having added seven properties aggregating 283 keys during the year across leisure, pilgrimage and urban markets, including Zone by The Park properties in Darjeeling, Gangtok and Katra and Zone Connect by The Park Patna in Bihar. The flagship project of the year was the integrated hospitality-led development on EM Bypass, Kolkata, comprising a 218-key hotel and 69 serviced apartments under the new THE Park UNIZEN branded-residence model, which uses residential sales to support development of the hospitality asset; 29 of the 69 apartments (42% of residential inventory) were booked at an average realisation of INR 20,857 per sq. ft., and the project is expected to generate INR 300-350 crores of cash flows over the next three years. The under-development pipeline stands at 43 hotels and 3,958 keys — THE Park Hotels (9 hotels, 1,430 keys), THE Park Collection (3 hotels, 91 keys), Zone by The Park (17 hotels, 1,455 keys) and Zone Connect by The Park (14 hotels, 982 keys) — weighted towards asset-light formats with 31 managed (2,814 keys) versus 7 owned (997 keys) and 5 leased (147 keys), taking the total intended portfolio to 85 hotels and 6,635 keys by FY 2029-30. Strategic projects at EM Bypass Kolkata, Juhu Mumbai, Visakhapatnam and Navi Mumbai are all in active stages of development: the Juhu property targets a launch in H2 FY28, ground construction is underway in Visakhapatnam, and progress continues across Pune and Navi Mumbai. At THE Park Visakhapatnam, site preparation and landscaping works are underway for an expansion that will add 100 new hotel rooms, a signature lounge, a luxury spa and a modern fitness centre; at THE Park Chennai The Residence Floor is being completely refurbished, and the Goa hotels plan to widen their F&B offerings. Inorganic expansion during the year included acquiring a 90% stake in the Juhu property via Zillion Hotels and Resorts, acquiring Purity on Lake Vembanad (including a luxury houseboat asset) and signing The Malabar House in Fort Kochi, Kerala (transaction expected to complete by October 2026), plus the addition of a property in Tranquebar, Tamil Nadu — all extending THE Park Collection. In retail F&B, Flurys grew to 110 outlets (44 cafés, 14 restaurants, 52 kiosks across seven states) after adding 10 outlets during the year, is on track to reach 120 stores shortly with more than 30 outlets planned across Delhi NCR, Pune and Bengaluru, targets around 140 outlets within 10 months and 150 in FY 2026-27, and holds an ambition to reach 200 stores by 2028 and to more than triple its footprint by the end of the decade. Operational build-out included the enterprise-wide rollout of SAP S/4HANA and deployment of the Nor1 AI-enabled upselling platform, alongside expansion to 4 IGBC-certified hotels.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:

- Multi-format, five-brand portfolio spanning luxury, boutique-heritage, upper-midscale and economy, plus branded residences — allowing the company to serve diverse demand segments from a single platform
- Experience-based F&B and entertainment platform: around 128 F&B outlets including Flurys, with F&B contributing 43% of total revenue and INR 303.8 crores of revenue in FY 2025-26
- Industry-leading operating metrics: national-high occupancy of 91% with RevPAR of INR 7,584 and an all-time-high ARR of INR 8,304, against national industry occupancy of 64% and ADR of INR 8,624

- Global design and hospitality recognition — Ran Baas The Palace awarded One MICHELIN Key, featured in Prix Versailles, Condé Nast Traveler HOT LIST and Architectural Digest's 2025 Great Design Hotel Awards; 30+ awards received during FY 2025-26

themes.title: Hospitality & travel up-cycle
themes.need: Q1FY27 split hotels from airlines. INDHOTEL delivered a 17th consecutive record quarter - consolidated revenue INR 2,419cr (+15%), EBITDA INR 753cr at 31.1%, standalone occupancy jumping to 82% from 76% on a 41.8% standalone EBITDA margin, and asset-light management-fee income INR 168cr (+26%) - with management now framing the West-Asia war as a NET tailwind because outbound travel stays home; leisure RevPAR (Rajasthan/Goa) ran up high-20s. Airlines got the mirror image: INDIGO's EBITDAR margin collapsed from 28.0% to 15.6% on blended ATF of ~INR 140-150/litre versus INR 85-90 pre-war (fuel CASK +~80% YoY), leaving yield as the only defence. MHRIL shows domestic leisure premiumisation is real - Keystone average unit realisation +73% to INR 14.4 lakh on stable gross sales. LEMONTREE/CHALET/SAMHI/THELEELA ride the same occupancy-led room cycle; TRAVELFOOD/TBOTEK/DREAMFOLKS remain levered to airport PAX and B2B travel.
themes.driver: Occupancy-led (not rate-led) RevPAR compounding plus INDHOTEL's Ginger conversion cadence stepping 15->20->25->40 per quarter through FY27; for airlines the swing is INDIGO's guided Q2 PRASK growth of 'more than 25%' on flattish capacity against ATF cracks.
